Adding Custom Feature Engineering Functions

Jenna Reps, Egill Fridgeirsson

2026-11-13

Source: vignettes/AddingCustomFeatureEngineering.Rmd
AddingCustomFeatureEngineering.Rmd

Introduction

This vignette describes how you can add your own custom function for feature engineering in the Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics (OHDSI) PatientLevelPrediction package. This vignette assumes you have read and are comfortable with building single patient level prediction models as described in the vignette('BuildingPredictiveModels').

We invite you to share your new feature engineering functions with the OHDSI community through our GitHub repository.

Feature Engineering Function Code Structure

To make a custom feature engineering function that can be used within PatientLevelPrediction you need to write two different functions. The ‘create’ function and the ‘implement’ function.

The ‘create’ function, e.g., create<FeatureEngineeringFunctionName>, takes the parameters of the feature engineering ‘implement’ function as input, checks these are valid and outputs these as a list of class ‘featureEngineeringSettings’ with the ‘fun’ attribute specifying the ‘implement’ function to call.

The ‘implement’ function, e.g., implement<FeatureEngineeringFunctionName>, is called twice: once on the training data, to learn what it needs and change the data, and again whenever the model is applied to new data, to make the same change there. It must take as input:

  • trainData - a list containing:

    • covariateData: the covariates. During training these are the covariates of the training patients. When the model is applied, they are the covariates of the data it is applied to, which can include patients outside the population being predicted.

    • labels: a data frame with one row per patient, containing rowId (patient identifier), the other columns of the study population such as ageYear and gender, and outcomeCount (the class labels) when it is known. When a model is applied to a full plpData without labels, for example by pfi(), labels is missing and cohorts holds the patients instead.

    • folds: a data frame that contains rowId (patient identifier) and index (the cross validation fold). This is only present during training.

  • featureEngineeringSettings - the output of your create<FeatureEngineeringFunctionName>

  • any further arguments you recorded during training (see below), such as values learned from the training data. Give them a NULL default: they are NULL during training and set when the model is applied to new data.

The ‘implement’ function can then do any manipulation of trainData$covariateData (adding new features or removing features). It should:

  1. Change trainData$covariateData directly. PatientLevelPrediction always passes data that it owns: during training this is the training set made when the data were split, and when a model is applied it is a copy made before the first step runs. You do not need to copy the data yourself, and the caller’s data is never changed.

  2. Call recordFeatureEngineeringStep() with the name of the ‘implement’ function and the arguments it needs to repeat the step on new data, typically the featureEngineeringSettings and the learned values. The model is saved as JSON, so these should be numbers, strings, logicals, data frames or lists of these, not fitted model objects.

  3. Return trainData.

When the model is applied to new data, PatientLevelPrediction calls each recorded step in the order it was recorded, with trainData and the recorded arguments.

Example

Let’s consider the situation where we wish to cap a continuous covariate at a quantile of its training values, so that extreme values do not dominate the model. The cap is learned from the training data and must be reused, not recomputed, when the model is applied to new data.

Create function

The inputs are the covariateId of the covariate to cap and the quantile to cap it at.

createCapCovariate <- function(covariateId, quantile = 0.99) {
  # create list of inputs to implement function
  featureEngineeringSettings <- list(
    covariateId = covariateId,
    quantile = quantile
  )

  # specify the function that will implement the feature engineering
  attr(featureEngineeringSettings, "fun") <- "implementCapCovariate"

  # make sure the object returned is of class "featureEngineeringSettings"
  class(featureEngineeringSettings) <- "featureEngineeringSettings"
  return(featureEngineeringSettings)
}

We now need to create the ‘implement’ function implementCapCovariate()

Implement function

The learned value is the cap. It is NULL during training, where it is computed from the training data, and it is the recorded value when the model is applied to new data.

implementCapCovariate <- function(trainData, featureEngineeringSettings, cap = NULL) {
  covariateId <- featureEngineeringSettings$covariateId

  # during training, learn the cap from the training data
  if (is.null(cap)) {
    cap <- trainData$covariateData$covariates |>
      dplyr::filter(.data$covariateId == !!covariateId) |>
      dplyr::pull(.data$covariateValue) |>
      stats::quantile(featureEngineeringSettings$quantile, names = FALSE)
  }

  # change the data in place
  trainData$covariateData$covariates <- trainData$covariateData$covariates |>
    dplyr::mutate(covariateValue = dplyr::if_else(
      .data$covariateId == !!covariateId & .data$covariateValue > !!cap,
      !!cap,
      .data$covariateValue
    ))

  # record how to repeat this step when the model is applied to new data
  trainData <- recordFeatureEngineeringStep(
    trainData,
    funct = "implementCapCovariate",
    settings = list(
      featureEngineeringSettings = featureEngineeringSettings,
      cap = cap
    )
  )

  return(trainData)
}

Using it

Pass the settings to runPlp() and turn feature engineering on in the execute settings. Here age (covariateId 1002) is capped at its 99th percentile in the training data:

capAge <- createCapCovariate(covariateId = 1002, quantile = 0.99)

plpResult <- runPlp(
  plpData = plpData,
  outcomeId = 3,
  featureEngineeringSettings = capAge,
  executeSettings = createExecuteSettings(
    runSplitData = TRUE,
    runFeatureEngineering = TRUE,
    runModelDevelopment = TRUE
  ),
  saveDirectory = file.path(tempdir(), "capAge")
)

The test set, predictPlp() and external validation then cap age at the value learned from the training data.
